newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Belgian SGB, GBL: a tale of two holdings.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Belgian SGB, GBL: a tale of two holdings.

text.p: Belgium may be home to many holding companies, but only two count: Societe Generale de Belgique SA (SGB) and Groupe Bruxelles Lambert SA (GBL).
Together they dominate this small country's economic landscape and their affiliates exercise control or have close links with 12 of Belgium's top 20 companies, ranked by market capitalisation.
If Luxembourg-based media holding Audiofina SA, a GBL fiefdom, is included the total goes up to 13. And on Tuesday they sealed the fate of utility group Tractebel SA.
But in style and substance the two companies could be world's apart and the distance would appear to be growing.

By selling its interests in Tractebel to SGB for 49 billion Belgian francs ($1.57 billion), the GBL group of self-made magnate Baron Albert Frere has cut one of its remaining links with Belgium's oldest company. SGB was founded in 1822, eight years before the Belgian state, to which it was indelibly linked for decades.

Strictly speaking, GBL is not directly involved in the transaction. SGB is acquiring its additional 24.47 percent of Tractebel for 20.38 percent from holding company Electrafina and for the rest via insurer Royale Belge.

However, Frere, sometimes referred to as the "man from Charleroi", the southern Belgian industrial town where he built his business empire in the 1960s, is known to be the dominant figure in the GBL group and in subsidiaries such as Electrafina.

"Frere has big money in his group...and behaves like a very influential, very dominant stock holder," one Belgian company chairman told Reuters on Wednesday. "He is a genius at manipulating people in a constructive way."
"He is a great buyer and seller...I hate to use the term wheeler-dealer, but that's what he is," one former business acquaintance said. "Everything he has is for sale."
SGB's stated policy at present is to support the development of its units, although it too has made a number of divestments in recent years, including cement firm CBR.

The GBL group acquired its shares in Tractebel in the wake of the 1988 takeover battle for control of SGB that pitted France's Cie. de Suez, supported by a number of Belgian investors, including Frere, against Italian businessman Carlo de Benedetti.
The battle was won by Suez, which remain's SGB's controlling shareholder with a little under 63 percent.

But why Frere decided to sell his Tractebel shares now remains unclear. Electrafina, which has netted 41 billion francs from the deal, said it has no immediate plans to spend the money, leaving room for speculation about the group's next move.
Frere himself does not give interviews and the group is notoriously guarded about its plans.
An obvious channel for investment is Luxembourg media group Cie. Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion (CLT), which Electrafina controls through Audiofina.
CLT recently struck an alliance with Germany's Bertelsmann group and is actively involved in discussions to launch a range of digital television programming.
One observer, citing recent press reports, said that perhaps the Belgian needs funds to buy out Canadian financier Paul Desmarais from their Swiss Pargesa joint venture.
Frere might also be preparing the ground for his departure from the financial stage, cleaning up his business empire before passing it on to his children, he added.
However another observer speculated that perhaps Frere's departure could be even more dramatic.

"I wonder if not one day there might be a merger between SGB and GBL. He's already a Baron and who knows, maybe they would make him a count if he organised the re-Belgianisation of SGB," he said, noting opposition in northern Dutch speaking areas of Belgium to French Suez's control.
